usage: The thing answered takes 에, not 을: 질문에 대답해요, never 질문을 대답해요
솔직하게 (honestly) and 정직하게 are the most common adverb partners
큰 소리로 / 작은 소리로 describe the manner of replying aloud
Phones are NOT 대답하다 — you 받다 (receive) a call; never 전화에 대답해요
examples: 네, 하고 대답했어요.
I answered, "Yes."
Simple: the bare reply 네 plus 대답하다 — this is how you report what someone said back
선생님 질문에 바로 대답했어요.
I answered the teacher's question right away.
Everyday: note 질문에 (에, the question you reply TO) and 바로 = right away
면접에서는 당황하지 말고 차분하게 대답하세요.
In the interview, don't panic — answer calmly.
Real situation: 차분하게 대답하다 is the set phrase for composed, measured replies
nuance: 대답하다 is 對答(대답)하다, the hanja 對 'facing' + 答 'reply', so it literally means to 'reply facing' a question — you give a verbal response back to something someone asked. The key boundary is against 답하다 and 응답하다: 대답하다 is the everyday spoken word (a child 대답해요 when called), 답하다 is more clipped and written (편지에 답하다 'reply to a letter'), and 응답하다 is formal/technical (서버가 응답하다 'the server responds'). The single biggest English-speaker trap is the particle: in English you 'answer the question' (direct object), but in Korean the question is the target you reply toward, so it MUST be 질문에 대답하다 with 에 — 질문을 대답하다 sounds clearly wrong to natives. Also note this is a 하다 verb, so every form is regular: 대답 + 해요, and the negative cleanly splits the noun off as 대답 안 해요 / 대답 못 해요. Do not stretch it to phones (use 전화를 받다) or to 'responding to email,' which Koreans handle with 답장하다.

Confusing 대답하다 (give an answer) with 질문하다 (pose a question) — they are opposite roles in a Q&A.

usage: I'm counting on you / nice to work with you
The single most-used set phrase — said when starting a job, a class, or any relationship
The listener 들어주다 (grants) the favor; 부탁을 들어주세요 = please grant my request
The person asked takes 에게/한테: 친구에게 부탁했어요
무리한 부탁 / 어려운 부탁 are common collocations for a big ask
examples: 이것 좀 부탁해.
Take care of this for me, please.
Simple: 좀 softens the ask between friends — banmal 부탁해 is casual but warm
바빠서 동생에게 설거지를 부탁했어요.
I was busy, so I asked my sibling to do the dishes.
Everyday: the task (설거지를) + the person (동생에게) both appear
부탁이 하나 있는데, 들어주실 수 있어요?
I have a favor to ask — could you grant it?
Real situation: the polite framing 부탁이 있는데 sets up a request before stating it
nuance: 부탁하다 is 付託(부탁)하다, hanja 付 'hand over' + 託 'entrust', so the image is entrusting a task into someone's hands — you are asking them to do something FOR you, leaning on their goodwill. Contrast it sharply with 요청하다 and 시키다: 부탁하다 is personal and humble (you owe a thank-you), 요청하다 is formal/institutional (자료를 요청하다 'request documents'), and 시키다 is to MAKE/order someone do it from a position of authority — never use 시키다 with someone older or you sound bossy. The famous phrase 잘 부탁합니다 has no clean English equivalent; it pre-thanks someone for the cooperation you're about to receive and is near-mandatory in introductions. English speakers misfire two ways: they try to use 부탁하다 to order food or goods (that is 주문하다), and they attach the favor with the wrong particle — the person is 에게/한테, and the favor itself, if stated, is the object: 친구에게 부탁을 했어요. As a 하다 verb it is fully regular, negating as 부탁 안 해요.

Marking the person with 을/를 (친구를 부탁해요 meaning 'ask the friend'). The person asked is 에게/한테: 친구에게 부탁해요. (친구를 부탁해요 instead means 'please look after my friend.')
Swapping in 시키다 to be polite. 시키다 means to order/make someone do it and sounds bossy to elders; humble requests use 부탁하다.

usage: 와/하고 marks the other party; here 약속 means an appointment to meet
keep a promise / keep an appointment
지키다 (guard) is THE verb for honoring it; 약속을 어기다 = break it
Attach -기로: 다시 만나기로 약속했어요 = promised to meet again
손가락(을) 걸다 = hook fingers; the childhood pinky promise
examples: 꼭 올게. 약속해!
I'll definitely come. I promise!
Simple: standalone 약속해! as an emphatic vow between friends
다음에 또 만나기로 약속했어요.
We promised to meet again next time.
Everyday: -기로 약속하다 is the pattern for promising an action
내일 두 시에 약속이 있어서 못 가요.
I have an appointment at two tomorrow, so I can't go.
Real situation: here the noun 약속 means a scheduled meet-up, not a vow
nuance: 약속하다 is 約束(약속)하다, hanja 約 'bind/pact' + 束 'tie up' — literally to 'bind and tie,' a vivid image of two people lashing their word together. The crucial thing for learners is that the noun 약속 carries TWO meanings that English splits: a 'promise' (a vow) and an 'appointment/plans' (a scheduled meeting). 친구와 약속이 있어요 means 'I have plans with a friend,' not 'I made a vow.' Contrast 약속하다 with 예약하다: 약속하다 is a person-to-person agreement to meet or to do something, while 예약하다 is to RESERVE a slot from a business (식당을 예약하다 'book a restaurant') — never say 식당을 약속하다. To promise an action, Koreans don't use the infinitive as in English ('promise to come'); they nominalize with -기로: 오기로 약속했어요. The verb honoring it is 지키다 (지키다, 'guard'), and breaking it is 어기다, so memorize 약속을 지키다/어기다 as a fixed pair. It is a regular 하다 verb (약속 + 해요), negating as 약속 안 해요.

usage: The person introduced is 을/를; the recipient is 에게/한테
자기소개 is one fixed noun; 자기소개 해 주세요 = please introduce yourself
소개 + 미팅; being set up romantically by a friend
By extension, 소개하다 = recommend/present a place or product
examples: 제 친구예요. 소개할게요.
This is my friend. Let me introduce you.
Simple: 소개할게요 (I'll introduce) used at the moment of presenting someone
남자친구를 부모님께 소개했어요.
I introduced my boyfriend to my parents.
Everyday: 을/를 for the person shown, 께 (honorific) for the parents who receive
좋은 책 좀 소개해 주실 수 있어요?
Could you recommend a good book?
Real situation: 소개하다 stretched to 'recommend' — common for books, shops, apps
nuance: 소개하다 is 紹介(소개)하다, hanja 紹 'connect/join' + 介 'go between', so the core sense is acting as a go-between who connects two parties — you present a person to someone else, or by extension present a place/product to an audience (recommend it). Watch the dual particle frame: the person or thing introduced takes 을/를, and the recipient takes 에게/한테 (honorific 께): 친구를 선생님께 소개했어요. Contrast 소개하다 with 추천하다: when recommending, 소개하다 means 'let me present/show you this option' (neutral introduction), while 추천하다 carries a stronger personal endorsement ('I vouch for it'). For introducing yourself, do not say 저를 소개해요 — Korean uses the set noun 자기소개를 하다. A culturally loaded offshoot is 소개팅 (소개 + meeting), being set up on a blind date by a mutual friend. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto 'meet' or 'greet': you 소개하다 (present) someone, but you 만나다 (meet) them and 인사하다 (greet) them — three different verbs. Regular 하다 verb: 소개 + 해요, negative 소개 안 해요.

Dropping the recipient particle or using 을/를 on both. The recipient is 에게/한테/께: 친구를 부모님께 소개했어요.
Confusing 소개하다 (present someone) with 만나다 (meet) or 인사하다 (greet) — introducing is not the same as meeting or saying hello.

usage: The thing explained takes 을/를: 이유를 설명해요
자세히 / 쉽게 / 간단히 are the habitual adverb partners
Use -에 대해(서) for the subject: 그 문제에 대해 설명했어요
사용법/방법 (method) commonly fill the object slot
examples: 이거 어떻게 해요? 설명해 줘.
How do I do this? Explain it to me.
Simple: casual 설명해 줘 — asking a friend to walk you through something
선생님이 문법을 쉽게 설명해 주셨어요.
The teacher explained the grammar to us simply.
Everyday: -아 주시다 shows the explaining was done as a favor by a senior
왜 늦었는지 자세히 설명해 주시겠어요?
Could you explain in detail why you were late?
Real situation: -는지 embeds the question being explained; 자세히 = in detail
nuance: 설명하다 is 說明(설명)하다, hanja 說 'speak' + 明 'bright/clear', so it literally means to 'speak something into clarity' — you talk about a thing so the listener understands it. The dividing line against 설득하다 and 말하다 matters: 설명하다 is to make something UNDERSTOOD (neutral, informational), 설득하다 is to PERSUADE (change someone's mind), and 말하다 is just to 'say/tell' without the goal of clarifying. So '설명해 주세요' = 'help me understand,' which is far more specific than '말해 주세요' = 'just tell me.' The thing explained takes 을/를 (이유를 설명하다), and for a broad topic Koreans add -에 대해(서): 그 사건에 대해 설명했어요. Natural adverbs are 자세히 (in detail), 쉽게 (simply), 간단히 (briefly). The English-speaker pitfall is the construction 'explain me' / 'explain to me' — Korean attaches the listener with 에게/한테, not the object slot, and very often just uses 설명해 주다 (explain as a favor) to imply the listener. It is a regular 하다 verb: 설명 + 해요, negating as 설명 안 해요 / 설명 못 해요.

Using 말하다 when you mean make-it-clear. 말하다 is merely 'say'; to clarify so someone understands, use 설명하다.
Confusing 설명하다 (explain) with 설득하다 (persuade) — explaining shares information; persuading changes a decision.

usage: 와/하고 marks the conversation partner; this is two-way chatting
In speech 이야기 → 얘기 almost always: 얘기 좀 해요
그 일에 대해 이야기했어요 = we talked about that matter
나누다 (share) is a slightly warmer, more literary partner verb
examples: 우리 이따가 얘기해.
Let's talk later.
Simple: contracted 얘기해 in banmal — exactly how friends actually speak
주말에 가족하고 많이 이야기했어요.
I talked a lot with my family over the weekend.
Everyday: 하고 = with; 많이 modifies the amount of talking
잠깐 따로 이야기 좀 할 수 있을까요?
Could we talk privately for a moment?
Real situation: 따로 (separately/privately) + 좀 softens a serious request to talk
nuance: 이야기하다 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) built from the noun 이야기 'a story/talk' + 하다, so at heart it means to exchange talk — to chat, converse, or tell about something. The contrast with 말하다 and 대화하다 is the thing to internalize: 말하다 is one-directional 'to say/tell' (a single utterance), 이야기하다 is the relaxed back-and-forth of chatting or recounting (often longer, with a partner marked by 와/하고), and 대화하다 is the more formal, neutral 'to converse/hold a dialogue.' So 친구와 이야기해요 feels friendly and chatty, while 대화해요 feels almost clinical. Massively important for sounding natural: in actual speech 이야기 contracts to 얘기 nearly every time — 얘기 좀 하자, 얘기해 줘. For talking ABOUT a topic, add -에 대해(서): 영화에 대해 이야기했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like one-shot 'tell me' — for a quick fact use 말해 줘, but for 'let's discuss / tell me the whole thing' use 이야기해 줘. It is a regular 하다 verb, negating as 이야기 안 해요.

Marking the partner with 을/를 (친구를 이야기해요). The conversation partner is 와/하고: 친구하고 이야기해요.

usage: The person greeted takes 에게/한테/께: 선생님께 인사했어요
Greeting in Korea is physical — a head bow, 고개를 숙이다, accompanies it
나누다 (share) for mutual greeting between two people
인사 specifies the type: 작별 인사 (farewell), 첫인사 (first greeting)
examples: 안녕하세요, 하고 인사했어요.
I greeted them, saying "Hello."
Simple: the greeting word 안녕하세요 reported with 인사하다
아이가 어른들께 공손히 인사했어요.
The child greeted the adults politely.
Everyday: 께 (honorific) + 공손히 (politely) — the respect register Korea expects
이사 와서 옆집에 가서 인사하고 왔어요.
I moved in and went next door to introduce myself / pay my respects.
Real situation: 인사하다 covers the courtesy visit to new neighbors
nuance: 인사하다 is 人事(인사)하다, hanja 人 'person' + 事 'affair' — literally 'the affairs between people,' which tells you it is broader than English 'greet': it covers saying hello, bowing, saying goodbye, and even paying one's formal respects. The person greeted takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께: 선생님께 인사했어요. Crucial cultural point baked into the verb: Korean greeting is physical and hierarchical — a younger person bows the head (고개를 숙이다) to an elder, and failing to 인사하다 first when meeting someone senior reads as rude. Contrast 인사하다 with 소개하다: greeting is the bow/hello you perform yourself, whereas introducing is presenting a third party. Note that the noun 인사 also means 'personnel/HR affairs' (인사부 = HR department) — same hanja, different sphere. The English-speaker pitfall is leaving out the bow-culture and treating it as a casual 'hi,' and also confusing it with the literal greeting words: 안녕하세요 is WHAT you say, 인사하다 is the act of greeting. It is a regular 하다 verb, negating as 인사 안 해요.

structuredNuance.t: 인사하다 is broader than English 'greet': it covers saying hello, bowing, saying goodbye, and even paying one's formal respects. The person greeted takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께: 선생님께 인사했어요. Crucial cultural point baked into the verb: Korean greeting is physical and hierarchical — a younger person bows the head (고개를 숙이다) to an elder, and failing to 인사하다 first when meeting someone senior reads as rude.

Contrast 인사하다 with 소개하다: greeting is the bow/hello you perform yourself, whereas introducing is presenting a third party. Note that the noun 인사 also means 'personnel/HR affairs' (인사부 = HR department) — same hanja, different sphere.
인사하다 is 人事(인사)하다, hanja 人 'person' + 事 'affair' — literally 'the affairs between people,' which tells you it is broader than English 'greet.'

usage: The person wronged takes 에게/한테/께: 친구에게 사과했어요
진심으로 (sincerely) / 정중히 (courteously) are the habitual adverbs
Give the cause with -아서: 늦어서 사과했어요 = apologized for being late
받아 주다 = graciously accept; 사과를 받아 주세요 = please accept my apology
examples: 미안해, 정말 사과할게.
I'm sorry, I sincerely apologize.
Simple: 사과할게 backs up the casual 미안해 with a fuller apology
제 실수라서 먼저 사과했어요.
It was my mistake, so I apologized first.
Everyday: -라서 gives the reason; 먼저 = first, taking the initiative
회사가 고객에게 공식적으로 사과했습니다.
The company formally apologized to its customers.
Real situation: 공식적으로 (formally) + 습니다 — the register of a public apology
nuance: 사과하다 is 謝過(사과)하다, hanja 謝 'express thanks/apology' + 過 'fault/error', so it literally means to 'acknowledge one's fault' — you take responsibility for a mistake to the person you wronged, who is marked with 에게/한테 or honorific 께. The boundary against 미안하다 and 변명하다 is essential: 미안하다 is the adjective/feeling 'to be sorry' (an emotional state — 미안해요), while 사과하다 is the ACT of formally apologizing (you can 사과하다 even publicly or in writing); and 변명하다 is the opposite move, to 'make excuses.' So you might 사과하다 instead of merely feeling 미안하다. The cause of the apology attaches with -아서: 늦어서 사과했어요. A notorious trap is the homograph: 사과 also means 'apple' (native-Korean noun), so context disambiguates 사과를 했어요 'apologized' from 사과를 먹었어요 'ate an apple' — they share spelling but are unrelated words. English speakers also wrongly say '~에 대해 미안해요' as if 'sorry' were a verb taking objects; to apologize FOR something, use 사과하다 with -아서 or -에 대해. Regular 하다 verb: 사과 + 해요, negative 사과 안 해요.

usage: The guest takes 을/를; the place/event takes 에: 친구를 집에 초대했어요
The event with 에 — common with 파티, 결혼식, 집들이
초대장 = the physical invite; 보내다 = send it
The set thank-you a guest says on arrival
examples: 내 생일에 너도 와. 초대할게!
Come to my birthday too. I'm inviting you!
Simple: casual 초대할게 — the moment of inviting a friend
집들이에 회사 동료들을 초대했어요.
I invited my coworkers to the housewarming.
Everyday: the guests (동료들을) + the event (집들이에) in the standard frame
저희 결혼식에 귀하를 정중히 초대합니다.
We courteously invite you to our wedding.
Real situation: the formal invitation-card register; 귀하 (honorific 'you') + 정중히 elevate the guest
nuance: 초대하다 is 招待(초대)하다, hanja 招 'beckon/summon' + 待 'receive/treat', so the image is beckoning someone over AND hosting them — inviting a guest to an event or your home with the intent to welcome and entertain them. The guest takes 을/를 and the event/place takes 에: 친구를 파티에 초대했어요. The sharp contrast is with 부르다: 초대하다 is a warm, planned invitation to a social occasion (you'll host them), whereas 부르다 is simply to 'call' someone over (call their name, summon them) with no hosting connotation — so 친구를 불렀어요 just means 'I called my friend over,' not 'I invited them to an event.' Using 부르다 where you mean a gracious invite sounds abrupt. Note the related noun 초대장 (invitation card) and the host's courtesy verb 모시다 for elevating an honored guest. The English-speaker pitfall is using 초대하다 for 'invite' in the loose sense of 'ask someone to come along casually' (that's closer to 같이 가자/오라고 하다), and forgetting that the EVENT is 에 while the guest is 을/를. Regular 하다 verb: 초대 + 해요, negative 초대 안 해요.

usage: The person praised takes 을/를: 아이를 칭찬했어요
받다 makes it passive: 선생님께 칭찬을 받았어요 = was praised by the teacher
아끼지 않다 (not spare) — a set phrase for praising freely
Literally 'until the mouth runs dry' — praise someone to the skies
examples: 잘했어! 정말 잘했다고 칭찬해 줬어요.
Well done! I praised them, saying they did great.
Simple: -다고 reports the praising words
선생님이 제 발표를 칭찬해 주셨어요.
The teacher praised my presentation.
Everyday: 을/를 for what's praised, -아 주시다 marks it as kindness from a senior
아이는 칭찬을 받을수록 더 잘해요.
The more a child is praised, the better they do.
Real situation: passive 칭찬을 받다 + -ㄹ수록 'the more...'
nuance: 칭찬하다 is 稱讚(칭찬)하다, hanja 稱 'state/declare' + 讚 'extol', so it means to openly declare someone's merit — to praise or commend a person for good work, effort, or behavior, with the person taking 을/를. The vital contrast is against 자랑하다: 칭찬하다 is praising SOMEONE ELSE for THEIR good qualities (외부를 향한 칭찬), whereas 자랑하다 is boasting about YOURSELF or your own things (자기 자랑). English 'praise' can blur into 'show off,' but in Korean these are firmly separate verbs — mixing them up reverses who's being celebrated. A second near-synonym is 칭찬 vs 격려하다 (encourage): 칭찬하다 rewards results already achieved, 격려하다 cheers someone on toward something. The passive 'to be praised' is 칭찬을 받다, not a verb ending. There is also a famous proverb-title 칭찬은 고래도 춤추게 한다 ('praise makes even a whale dance'), capturing its motivational power. The English-speaker pitfall is using 칭찬하다 for complimenting an object directly (the food, the weather) — for a casual compliment Koreans more often just say 멋있다/예쁘다 or use 칭찬 about a person's achievement. Regular 하다 verb: 칭찬 + 해요, negative 칭찬 안 해요.

usage: The person lied to takes 에게/한테: 친구에게 거짓말했어요
Can split the noun: 거짓말을 했어요 (object form, slightly more emphatic)
새빨간 (bright red) 거짓말 — set phrase for an outright lie
들통나다/들키다 = be found out; 거짓말이 들통났어요
examples: 거짓말하지 마.
Don't lie.
Simple: blunt banmal prohibition — said when you catch someone fibbing
동생이 엄마한테 거짓말했어요.
My sibling lied to Mom.
Everyday: 한테 (casual 'to') marks who was lied to
그 사람은 눈 하나 깜짝 안 하고 거짓말해요.
That person lies without batting an eye.
Real situation: idiom 눈 하나 깜짝 안 하다 for lying shamelessly
nuance: 거짓말하다 is a native Korean compound: 거짓 'false' + 말 'speech/words' = 'false words,' plus 하다 — so it transparently means 'to do false-speech,' i.e. to tell a lie. It is built on the noun 거짓말, which is why the negative and the 못 form split the noun cleanly off the verb: 거짓말 안 해요, 거짓말 못 해요. The person lied to takes 에게/한테. Contrast it with 속이다 and 농담하다: 거짓말하다 is the act of stating an untruth (the words themselves are false), 속이다 is 'to deceive/trick' (to fool someone, broader than just words — you can 속이다 with actions), and 농담하다 is 'to joke,' which is harmless and not meant to be believed. Calling a joke a 거짓말 sounds like an accusation. A natural intensifier is 새빨간 거짓말 ('a bright-red lie' = a barefaced lie). The English-speaker pitfall is the reflex 'lie about something' — Korean doesn't take 'about' here; you simply 거짓말하다 and add context separately, or use 거짓말로 ... 하다. Also note English 'lie' looks intransitive but Korean often makes the lie an explicit object: 거짓말을 하다. It is a regular 하다 verb.

usage: The person asked takes 에게/한테/께: 선생님께 질문했어요
The most common framing: 질문 있어요? = any questions?
받다 for receiving questions: 질문을 받겠습니다 = I'll take questions
그 점에 대해 질문했어요 = I asked about that point
examples: 하나 질문해도 돼요?
May I ask one question?
Simple: the polite opener for raising a hand in class
수업 끝나고 선생님께 질문했어요.
I asked the teacher a question after class.
Everyday: 께 (honorific) marks the senior being asked
발표 후에 청중에게서 질문을 많이 받았어요.
After the presentation I got a lot of questions from the audience.
Real situation: passive 질문을 받다 + 에게서 'from'
nuance: 질문하다 is 質問(질문)하다, hanja 質 'inquire into substance' + 問 'ask', so it means to pose a question in order to obtain information — and the person asked takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께: 선생님께 질문했어요. The boundary against 묻다 is the one to nail: 질문하다 and 묻다 both mean 'ask,' but 질문하다 is the heavier Sino-Korean word for a deliberate, often public question (in class, a meeting, a Q&A), while 묻다 is the plain everyday verb for asking a quick thing ('let me ask you something' = 뭐 좀 물어볼게요). You would not say 길을 질문하다 for 'ask directions' — that's 길을 묻다. Note 묻다 is itself a ㄷ-irregular verb (묻다 → 물어요), whereas 질문하다, being a 하다 verb, is perfectly regular (질문 + 해요). 질문하다 is also the exact opposite of 대답하다 (to answer) — they are the two roles in a Q&A. The English-speaker pitfall is forcing a direct object: you don't 'ask a question to someone' with 을/를 on the person; the question can be the object (질문을 하다) but the person is 에게/께. Receiving questions is 질문을 받다. Regular 하다 verb, negative 질문 안 해요.
